Why Is Holi Celebrated? — Teaching Kids All About The Festival Of Colours
Ever wondered why Holi is celebrated as the festival of colours all over India? Read on to know about the importance of Holi, the legends surrounding it, and different rituals/celebrations associated with this Hindu Festival…
‘Diversity’ perfectly defines the culture and way of life in India. Being a country rooted in traditions, miscellaneous customs & celebrations bring the entire population together. From ancient legends to religious rituals, shifting seasons to social practices and unique observances- India’s kaleidoscopic cultural potpourri bedazzles visitors, finding a reason to celebrate hope, happiness & positive emotions by means of festivals. And what better way to celebrate the Indian diversity than with colours- probably one of the reasons why we celebrate Holi!
Why Do We Celebrate Holi — The Festival Of Colours?
There are innumerable reasons behind celebrating Holi, the most important one being that it is the expression of togetherness & acceptance. According to the Indian Shaka calendar, Holi is celebrated in Phalgun on a full moon day during the spring season, which marks the end of cold winters and welcomes spring, thus, symbolising new beginnings. Holi reflects the deeper themes in life- the joy of having friendships, the triumph of good over evil, the expression of positive emotions, the strength to overcome challenges, negativities, arguments, or bitterness in relationships, and to move on with positive emotions.
Holi 2021 Date: This year, the festival of Holi falls on the 28th and 29th of March.
Holi Legends: The Story Of Holi Festival
Figure 1: The story of Prahlad and Holika
The story of demon king Hiranyakashyap and his son Prahlad is one of the famous legends surrounding Holi. The ruthless Hiranyakashyap wanted his subjects to worship him as the God but his son, being an ardent devotee of Lord Vishnu refused to follow his orders. The proud king decided to punish Prahlad’s misdemeanour by ordering him to sit on a burning pyre with his aunt Holika. It was a conspiracy to kill Prahlad and a test of his devotion since Holika had a boon. Hirankashyap’s sister possessed a special cloak that provided her protection against fire. However, when she entered into the fire wrapped in the cloak, with Prahlad sitting in her lap, the wind blew away the cloak that landed on her nephew. Thus, Prahlad survived because of his faith & devotion, whereas Holika burned to ashes- an incident that symbolises the triumph of good over evil.
That’s how the custom of celebrating Holika Dahan came into existence. On the first day of Holi (known as Chhoti Holi or Holika Dahan ), an effigy of Holika made out of cow dung is burned on a woodpile, along with other old, worn, and waste items-a practice that reminds us to do away with all the negativity in life.
Figure 2: The story of Holi — Why is Lath Mar Holi celebrated in Mathura?
Another story of Holi is based on the life of little Krishna. Lord Krishna, in his childhood, was upset because of his friends mocking his dark complexion and pleaded his complaint before his mother Yashodha. To cheer him up, Yashodha replied that he could colour his friends in any hue of his choice. The mischievous young lord decided to visit Barsana (a village in Mathura) to spray colours on his friends and the village Gopis (milkmaids). However, the women were angered by his prank and chased him away with batons (wooden sticks) — an event that evolved into the practice of Lath Mar Holi. It is still observed in Mathura and some parts of UP on the 2nd day of Holi when people spray colours on each other. The women chase and playfully hit the men with wooden sticks whereas the men try to escape them. The man or boy who is caught by the females is made to dance like a woman. This social custom is a jest, performed without any hard or aggressive feelings.
How Do We Celebrate Holi? — 8 Different Types Of Holi Celebrations In India
Indians celebrate Holi in different ways, as per their local customs and traditions. Here are some beautiful ways in which the festival of colour is celebrated.
Baithaki/Khadi Holi/Kahila HoliIn Uttarakhand
Holi is the occasion of strengthening social bonds for the people of Uttarakhand. On the day of Holi, people form small groups, dress in traditional attires & roam around the city. Friends and neighbours conduct Baithaks (group meetings) where people sing traditional songs, smear colour on each other’s’ faces, and enjoy traditional sweets.
Basant Utsav In West Bengal
Basant Utsav celebrates the arrival of Rituraj Basant (Spring- the king of all seasons). People dress up in yellow-coloured clothes (a symbol of blooming mustard flowers), gather in the temples to sing, dance. and sprinkle Gulaal (powdered colours) on each other.They also perform Dol Jatras (Street Performances) where artists recite Rabindranath Tagore’s poems & perform on traditional songs.
Dola In Orissa
Figure 3: Dola celebration in Orissa
Dola Holi celebration in Orissa lasts for a week, starting on Falgun Dashmi where the people participate in Rath Yatra (temple processions) taken out in the name of Lord Jagannath (believed to be an avatar of Krishna). The grand tour covers different parts of the city during which devotees sprinkle Abira (coloured powder) on the passer-by and offer them sweets.
Holla Mohalla in Punjab
The brave hearts of Punjab observe Pariva (the 3rd day of Holi) as a day commemorating the bravery of ancient Sikh Warriors. The Nihang tribe of Sikhs, who are adept in martial arts, perform traditional warfare on horseback, sing & dance in groups.
Shigmo Parade in Goa
The farmers of Goa welcome the spring with a parade & street carnival. They thank the Lord for a bountiful harvest, sing traditional hymns, and perform folk dances to celebrate.
Shimga/Rang Panchami in most of Northern States
Many of the northern Indian states celebrate Holi for 2 days. On the first day of Holi, they light a sacred fire symbolising Holika Dahan & thank the harvest god for blessing them with surplus yield. The next day is celebrated as Rang Panchami (or Pakuwah in Assam) where people gather in a public setting to play colours, sing & dance.
People of Bihar & Jharkhand celebrate Holi as Phagunwa, which is similar to the 2-day Holi celebration. The only difference is that they recite local legends and tales in Bhojpuri language and the women prepare Gujhiyas & Thandais to welcome guests.
Ukuli or Manjal Kuli in Kerala
Traditional dishes prepared during Holi
The Konkani & Kumba communities of Kerala celebrate Holi or Ukuli/Manjal Kuli with yellow colour (an auspicious hue symbolising happiness and positivity). They spray ground turmeric (Manjal Kuli) on one another and pray for their well-being.
Yoasang in Manipur
The people of Manipur celebrate Holi for six days but the most important ritual (Yoasand) is observed on the last full moon day of Phalgun. The youth construct roadside bamboo huts as a part of this ritual and a Brahmin (Hindu priest) places the idol of Lord Chaitanya inside the hut. The idol is worshipped for five days, bhajans and kirtan performed by men & women. On the sixth day, the idol is transferred to the temple and the hut is set on fire. People sing& dance around the fire, chanting ‘He Hari’ & ‘Hari Bola’. Following a Puja in Govind Jee temple, people spray coloured water on one another and sing the praise of Lord Krishna.
Why Do We Play Colours On Holi?
Colour psychology believes that every shade in this world has a deep meaning behind it and emits rays of different wavelengths that affect living beings around them. The bright and playful colours of Holi have the following meaning:
Figure 5: Children celebrating Holi
Yellow — Hope
Orange — Happiness
Red — Love
Pink — Positivity
Green — Abundance
Blue —
